author: Thomas Taylor

title: Introduction to the Hipparchus
printed: The Works of Plato, translated by Floyer Sydenham and Thomas Taylor, vol. V (London, 1804), pp. 356-356
anchoring: An introduction to the whole dialogue: each paragraph is a note on the whole Hipparchus. Taylor's footnotes to it are kept with the paragraph they are printed under.

notes.text: IL n E design of the Hipparchus is to show that all men naturally desire oQod, since even those who wander from it through avarice, wander throuo^h a desire of obtainhig it; but they err in consequence of mistaking good, which is a mean for ultimate good. For good is two-fold, one being the end, the other subsisting for the sake of the end. Hence the possession of the former is called beatitude^ and of the latter gain. Hence too, gain is the acquisition of that good, which contributes to the possession of ultimate good But that which does not contribute to this, is neither useful, nor is the acquisition of it gain. The desire therefore of gain thus defined, and which is naturally inherent in all men, is laudable; but the false opinion is to be reprobated, which, while it is ignorant of the truly useful and lucrative, dillorts to things adverse the natural appetite of man. Plato latently teaches this, while he confutes the false definitions which are introduced in this Dialogue, concerning the desire of gain. But he employs this proposition, that all men desire good as manifefi:, in order to conclude that all men naturally desire gain, and that this natural desire is laudable. And this is tiie conckifion which Socrates after a manner diredly introduces by three modes of arguing, viz. by example, by induction, and by reasoning. But from the whole Dialogue we collect, that all men desire good; and this is its ultimate end. For its first end is to Show that all men are desirous of gain, and that this desire is not to be blamed when directed to gain according to its true definition.
